extracted.intended_audience: Hollywood Reporter readers; general audience and entertainment industry readers interested in late-night comedy and Stephen Colbert
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical principles (implicit and explicit) about performing, writing, and producing late-night/television comedy, plus career/legacy considerations for a late-night host transitioning to other projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize the joke / 'your standard is the joke'
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s important to never forget that your standard is the joke... What’s funny about this?” — comedy’s primary standard is whether something is funny, not whether it advances an agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humor as the primary evaluative lens; keep the joke central when choosing material. Anti-pattern: prioritizing politics or messaging over comedic payoff. Scoring note: material should be judged first by its funniness and whether it lands as a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not encourage booing; 'Don't boo, laugh.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage instruction to audiences: “Don’t boo, laugh.” Booing ‘sounds like we’re cheering for sides’ and can ‘step on setups and punchlines.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage audience behavior to preserve timing and comedic structure. Explicitly discourage boos because they interrupt setups/punchlines and change the tone from laughter to partisan cheering. Example: telling audiences not to boo when the target is a political figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning comedy into an agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Colbert: If people think I’m 'on some kind of agenda' then I’m bad at it; don't delude yourself that there is any part of the job other than making the audience laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep satire and topical material focused on humor rather than trying to effect political change. Anti-pattern: making the show primarily an agenda vehicle instead of a source of jokes; this reduces comedic effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat adaptations as drama, not fandom
rubrics_metrics.description: On writing for Lord of the Rings: 'Follow your heart and the craft to try to turn this into something that is not fandom but drama,' and work with experienced creators (e.g., Philippa Boyens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting beloved material, prioritize dramatic storytelling and craft over fan-service or celebrity entitlement. Bring on veterans of the property to ensure respect for source material and quality. Anti-pattern: relying on fame/superfan status alone as justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor collaborative formats over solo stand-up when that’s your strength
rubrics_metrics.description: “Improv is collaborative in its nature, and all the shows that I’ve done have been collaborative... It’s not like I’m going to go out tomorrow and do a tight 10 at Zanies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose performance formats that align with your skills and history—if your work has been ensemble/collaborative, consider creating shows or collaborative projects rather than traditional stand-up. Example: creating a show or co-writing rather than pursuing a stand-up circuit career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not revive satirical characters unless they can outpace reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Colbert declined reviving his Colbert Report character because he couldn’t 'leapfrog the mendacity of the public discourse' — satire must be able to surpass the outrageousness of reality to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a satirical persona still provides critical distance and comedic advantage; if reality has become more extreme than the caricature, revival may fail. Anti-pattern: reusing old characters without checking if context still supports satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for a comedic legacy—be remembered as a comedy show
rubrics_metrics.description: He wants to be 'remembered as a comedy show' and emphasizes 'we harvest laughter for a living.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize lasting comedic quality and audience appreciation over short-term controversies or other measures of success. Legacy-oriented choices should favor consistent comedic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of network/business constraints and model realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of CBS/Paramount decisions, ad rates, differentiation from previous shows, and the collapsing broadcast model: networks have financial and strategic constraints that shape content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing TV comedy, account for business realities (contracts, ad rates, network directives). Anticipate limits on topicality and format imposed by platforms and negotiate within those constraints rather than assuming creative freedoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate industry relationships and use experienced collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Colbert references conversations with peers (Jon Stewart, Conan), working with a seasoned co-writer (Philippa Boyens), and outreach to executives as part of career moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage professional networks for career transitions, creative partnerships, and access to projects. Example: pairing a celebrity-superfan writer with a franchise veteran to produce credible adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use timing and life perspective when planning exits/transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Colbert notes life events (family wedding, son’s graduation) giving perspective, and that knowing an end in advance allows for material and stance; unexpected endings can be reframed as opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan show endings/transitions to preserve material and tone; when endings are unexpected, use them to create new comedic opportunities (e.g., 'jokes about the end of the show'). Anti-pattern: ignoring personal timing or failing to repurpose a forced exit.
